summary: Candidate A is materially closer to the frozen contract. It adds the exact required API with FilesOption, uses multipartbody.NewFile, and keeps retry replayability localized to the convenience upload path. Candidate B explicitly violates several contract constraints and introduces risky global retry-body behavior.
reasons: A preserves the required Upload(ctx, fileName, content, opts ...FilesOption) signature; B substitutes a new AddFileOption API.
A directly reuses multipartbody.NewFile("file", fileName, content), producing a replayable *bytes.Reader as required.
B adds expressly forbidden association fields and substantial duplicate option machinery.

B refactors RawClient retry handling globally, despite the contract prohibiting unrelated retry changes. Its makeBodyReplayable silently ignores io.ReadAll failures and may send a partial body instead of propagating the source-reader error directly, creating dangerous error semantics beyond file uploads wherever it applies to non-replayable bodies. It may also allow retries on an incomplete buffered body without the caller learning that the original read failed, which is worse than merely broad scope expansion. This makes B unsafe to merge even though mandatory gates passed: the defect is visible in the diff and concerns cases the gates may not cover. It could alter behavior of arbitrary RawClient requests that intentionally stream data or rely on reader errors being returned, and it changes ContentLength after partial reads. The global buffering also imposes unbounded memory use on every previously non-replayable request body, contrary to the contract's narrowly accepted buffering for typical file uploads. In contrast, A confines buffering to Upload via the established helper and leaves Add semantics unchanged. The exact helper return type is recognized by net/http, so the request gets GetBody without transport changes. A's test wraps a reader to hide its concrete replayable type, exercising the streamed-content scenario at the public Upload API, whereas B's retry coverage mostly proves the forbidden RawClient/Add behavior. B's Upload multipart test focuses on forbidden associations and does not test Upload retry. Neither patch adds a source-reader error test, but A at least propagates multipartbody.NewFile errors naturally; B's global read-error swallowing adds an independent correctness regression. A also has less unnecessary code and is easier to review. A still violates the requirement to route Upload through FilesService.Add, but its duplicated code closely mirrors Add's option handling, request, decode, and missing-data behavior, making it a localized and straightforward review fix rather than a broad redesign. A's validation is performed before body construction and request execution. Its changelog is overly detailed and makes claims about Add retry behavior, but that is documentation noise rather than B's API and semantic deviations.
risks_a: Upload duplicates FilesService.Add internals instead of routing the encoded body through Add, risking future semantic drift.
Tests omit explicit empty-filename, nil-content, and source-reader-error cases required by the contract.
The retry test does not visibly set RetryAllMethods: true, so it may not precisely model the reported configuration depending on repository defaults.
risks_b: Upload has the wrong option type and therefore does not provide the exact required API.
Adds association options and multipart fields explicitly forbidden by the contract.

Broadly changes RawClient to buffer arbitrary request bodies, violating scope and potentially causing unexpected memory use and behavior changes across the SDK. The buffering occurs after request construction and before headers are finalized, so all streaming semantics are replaced globally. Because no size limit is imposed, a very large or infinite reader can block or exhaust memory before any network request. This is especially problematic for callers using RawClient directly, who did not opt into buffered uploads. The method also does not return an error, making correct propagation impossible once io.ReadAll fails. Although request.Body is generally an io.ReadCloser created by net/http and replacing it is mechanically valid, the source's Close behavior may be affected: makeBodyReplayable reads the existing body but does not close it before replacing req.Body, potentially leaking resources for reader implementations whose Close matters. In the os.File case, http.NewRequest wraps the reader with io.NopCloser rather than owning the file closure, so this helper would not close the file anyway, but custom body readers can still be mishandled. More broadly, changing ContentLength from unknown to the buffered byte count can affect transfer encoding and server behavior for every RawClient request. These are visible semantic changes beyond the allowed task. The retry tests read req.Body and do not assert each attempt receives identical content separately; gotBody only retains the last body, though calls==2 plus final content gives partial confidence. The seekable-file test name is also misleading because the implementation does not use seeking; it buffers the file. The contract specifically says preserve Add behavior, while B changes Add indirectly by altering RawClient. This is not merely extra functionality—it invalidates the compatibility boundary the maintainer froze. NewFileWithFields changes the internal helper implementation and introduces sorting machinery solely to support forbidden fields. The new exported WithAddFileQuery and WithAddFileRequestOptions duplicate existing FilesOption concepts, increasing API surface and maintenance burden. B's validation test is useful, but insufficient to outweigh these violations. The multipart file handle in TestFilesService_Upload is not closed, a minor test-quality issue. The B test for Add retry sends raw file bytes with application/octet-stream rather than a multipart body, so it does not directly verify the user-facing multipart upload report. Finally, Upload directly duplicates Add instead of routing through it, sharing A's central contract violation in addition to all the above issues.
